study.title: Jeremiah 5 - General corruption, deserved judgment and denunciation of religious leaders
study.overview: Jeremiah 5 presents a comprehensive accusation against Judah and Jerusalem. The prophet unsuccessfully seeks one who does justice and seeks the truth; shows that poor and powerful equally corrupted themselves; he announces that infidelity, idolatry and immorality attract severe judgment; and concludes by denouncing false prophets, dominating priests, and a people who accept this situation. At the same time, the chapter preserves a flash of mercy: God will not make a total extermination.

outline.title: Absence of justice and corruption at all levels
outline.explanation: Jeremiah is sent to seek in Jerusalem anyone who does justice and seeks the truth, but the city is marked by false oaths and resistance to correction. The prophet first thinks of the poor, then the great ones; but both groups broke the yoke of obedience. Therefore, the image of the attack of beasts expresses an inevitable judgment on a society that multiplied its transgressions and infidelities.

outline.title: Infidelity, spiritual adultery, and denial of judgment
outline.explanation: The Lord asks how he could forgive a people who forsaken Him, swore for false gods, and gave themselves up to idolatry and adultery. The guilt is described as betrayal of the covenant: Judah and Israel deny the Lord and reject the prophetic warnings, treating the words of the prophets as a wind. The result is that God's own words become a consuming fire, and the enemy is announced as an instrument of judgment.

outline.title: Judgment coming from afar, but not total destruction
outline.explanation: God declares that He will do His words in Jeremiah as fire, while the people will be wood. A strong and ancient nation, of a strange language, will come and devour harvest, flocks and fortified cities. Still, the Lord says that he will not end the people completely. When the question comes about the reason for the punishment, Jeremiah must answer that the same logic of infidelity is fulfilled: whoever has abandoned the Lord and served foreign gods will serve foreigners in a foreigner land.

outline.title: Call to the fear of God and denunciation of false leaders
outline.explanation: Jeremiah must proclaim to the people that he is foolish and without understanding: he sees and hears, but he does not realize what God has done, including the sea subjected to the limit established by the Creator. The people are called to fear the Lord, who give the rain in the right time and sustain the harvest; but their sins have turned away good. The final section exposes social perversity: men arm ties, enrich by mistake, neglect orphans and needy, and the cuspid of shame is that prophets lie, priests rule by their own hands and the people approve of it. The final question shows that this trajectory ends in disaster.

study.context: The chapter speaks to Judah and Jerusalem within the framework of Jeremiah's preaching to the house of Israel and to the house of Judah. The text presupposes a visible religious society, with prophets and priests, but morally corrupted. The notes provided highlight the falsehood of the oath, the refusal to receive correction, the threat of an enemy from outside and the denunciation of religious leaders who deform their function.
study.theology: Jeremiah 5 teaches that God does not judge by whim, but in response to the rupture of the covenant, to religious lies and social injustice. The truth before God includes integrity in speaking, fidelity in worship and concrete justice in public life. The chapter also shows that sin hardens consciousness: the people not only err, but resist correction and prefer leaders to confirm their rebellion. At the same time, divine mercy does not disappear: judgment is real, but it is not absolute destruction. Theologically, the fear of the Lord appears as a principle of restoration, for recognizing the Creator and his ordinances should lead to obedience, gratitude, and reverence.

scholarViews.insight: The search for righteousness in Jerusalem fails: neither honesty nor sincerity is found, and even the oaths of the people are false.
Even after being wounded by disasters, the people remain without repentance and refuse God's correction.
The reference to the false prophets shows that they announced favorable things to please both the princes and the people.

questions: In which areas does my faith run the risk of being only appearance, without truth practice before God?
Have I accepted the correction of the Lord or hardened the heart when I am confronted with my sin?
How can I reject leaders and messages that please sin instead of leading to fear of God?
study.practice: Examine your life in the light of this chapter: speak the truth, practice justice, reject any form of faith of facade and submit your heart to the fear of the Lord. It is also worth reviewing which voices you follow: not every religious leadership is faithful, and the people of God should not approve what removes them from obedience. In concrete terms, pray for discernment, treat people under their responsibility and accept God's discipline before it becomes more severe judgment.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain in detail all the symbols of the chapter, such as the beasts, the nation from afar or the image of fire and firewood; therefore, the reading here is summarized and limited to what the text and the comments quoted state. Nor should the exact identification of all the groups mentioned in the prophetic images be treated as an indisputable fact, because the notes present these expressions as language of judgment and not as an exhaustive description.
